double-pointer.body:
C passes by value, always. `void f(t_list *lst)` receives a copy of the head pointer; assigning
to it changes nothing the caller can see. `void f(t_list **lst)` receives the address of the
caller's variable, and `*lst = new` writes through to it.

The other instance is shape rather than mutation: `char **` is a `NULL`-terminated array of
`char *`, each element separately allocated — two levels of ownership, two levels of cleanup.

double-pointer.title: To change the caller's pointer, you need the address of the caller's pointer.

fd-io.body:
`0` stdin, `1` stdout, `2` stderr. `ssize_t write(int fd, const void *buf, size_t count)` is the
only output primitive Part 2 may use (Subject IV.3) — no `printf`, no `putchar`. These functions
have no return value, so the only observable is what appeared on the descriptor.

A corollary worth knowing: a forgotten debug `printf` inside a libft function is invisible in
your own testing and glaring in an evaluation.

fd-io.title: `write` is a system call, and a file descriptor is just a small integer.

function-pointer.body:
```c
char (*f)(unsigned int, char);   /* pointer to a function taking (uint, char), returning char */
f(i, s[i]);                       /* call it — the & and * are optional */
```

It separates *iteration* from *transformation*: `ft_strmapi` knows how to walk a string, the
callback knows what to do with a character, and neither knows about the other. The same idea
carries `del` into `ft_lstclear` and `f` into `ft_lstiter`.

Read the declaration outward from the identifier: `f` is a pointer, to a function, taking
`(unsigned int, char)`, returning `char`.
defense: What is the type of the second parameter of `ft_strmapi`, in words?
function-pointer.title: A parameter that is code.

int-min.body:
Two's complement is asymmetric: `INT_MIN` is −2147483648, `INT_MAX` is 2147483647. Negating
`INT_MIN` overflows, which is undefined behaviour rather than merely a wrong number. `n = -n` as
the first line of `ft_itoa` or `ft_putnbr_fd` is the most common crash in the project.

Three legitimate answers: promote to `long`, do the arithmetic in `unsigned`, or special-case
`INT_MIN`. All three are fine; being able to say which you chose is the point.

`ft_atoi` meets it from the other end — `"-2147483648"` must parse, so the accumulator cannot be
a plain positive `int`.
int-min.title: `-(-2147483648)` does not fit in an `int`.

int-promotion.body:
`memset(void *, int c, size_t)`, `memchr(const void *, int c, size_t)`, `strchr(const char *,
int c)` all convert `c` to a character before using it. That is why `ft_strchr(s, 't' + 256)`
finds `'t'` and `ft_memset(buf, 0x1FF, n)` fills with `0xFF`.

The `ft_is*` family is the mirror: they take `int` so they can accept `EOF` and the full
`unsigned char` range, and must return 0 for everything outside it.

whole `ft_is*` / `ft_to*` family
int-promotion.title: Several libc functions take an `int` and use only its low byte.

list-ownership.body:
| | frees the node | frees the content |
|---|---|---|
| `ft_lstdelone` | ✔ `free` | ✔ via `del` |
| `ft_lstclear` | ✔ every node | ✔ via `del`, every node |
| `ft_lstiter` | ✘ | ✘ |
| `ft_lstnew` | — | takes ownership of the *pointer*, does not copy |

Two rules that are graded. The content is freed with the caller's `del`, never with `free`
directly — the caller may have allocated it in a way `free` cannot undo. And `ft_lstclear` must
set `*lst = NULL`, or the caller is left holding a pointer into freed memory. Pitfall **P5**.

malloc-rollback.body:
```
s_array ──▶ [ ptr0 | ptr1 |  ✗   | NULL ]
              │      │
              ▼      ▼
           "hello" "world"      ← nobody else holds these pointers
```

Nothing in the program has another reference to those words. Returning `NULL` without freeing
them is a permanent leak, and it is invisible to any test that does not force the failure.

`ft_lstmap` is the harder case: the partially built list needs `del` for each content *and*
`free` for each node.

malloc-rollback.title: If allocation *n* fails, allocations 1..n−1 are yours to free.

null-terminator.body:
`malloc(strlen(s))` is one byte short of a string. It usually appears to work, because the byte
after your allocation is usually already zero — right up until it is not, and then it fails on
the evaluator's machine and not yours. Pitfall **P1**.

over-allocation.body:
`ft_substr("hello", 1, 1000000000)` must allocate 5 bytes, not a gigabyte. The requested `len` is
a maximum; the real size is `min(len, strlen(s) - start) + 1`. With `len = SIZE_MAX` a naive
implementation asks the kernel for 18 exabytes and gets `NULL` — which then looks like an
allocation bug rather than the arithmetic bug it is.

`ft_calloc` is the same idea from the other side: `nmemb * size` can overflow, so check
`nmemb > SIZE_MAX / size` *before* multiplying.
defense: How many bytes does `ft_substr(s, 1, SIZE_MAX)` allocate?
over-allocation.title: Allocate what you need, not what you were asked for.

overlap.body:
```
src = buf, dst = buf + 2, n = 5, buf = "abcde"

forward:  buf[2] = buf[0]   "abade"    ← 'c' is gone; step 3 still needs it
          buf[3] = buf[1]   "ababe"
          buf[4] = buf[2]   "ababa"    ← reads the 'a' it wrote at step 1  ✗

correct:  "ababc"                       backward, from the last byte down
```

`memcpy` may assume the regions are disjoint and is optimised on that promise. `memmove` must
cope: when `dst > src`, copy from the end backward.
defense: What is the difference between `memcpy` and `memmove`?
overlap.title: Copying forward through overlapping memory destroys what you have not read yet.

pointer-arith.body:
Adding 1 to a `char *` moves one byte; adding 1 to an `int *` moves four. `end - start` is the
number of elements between them — which is the whole length calculation in `ft_substr` and
`ft_strtrim`, and the reason both are three lines once you see it.

pointer-arith.title: A pointer is an address; subtracting two of them gives a count.

return-contract.body:
- `ft_is*` return strictly `1` or `0` — not "any non-zero" (Subject IV.2 note).
- `ft_strlcpy` / `ft_strlcat` return **the length they tried to create**, which is how the caller
  detects truncation — not the length they actually wrote.
- `ft_strlcat` specifically: when `size <= strlen(dst)`, nothing is appended and the return is
  `size + strlen(src)`.
- `ft_calloc(0, 0)` returns a unique non-`NULL` pointer that `free()` accepts.
- `ft_substr` with `start >= strlen(s)` returns an allocated `""`, not `NULL`.
- `ft_strncmp` / `ft_memcmp` specify only the **sign**; testing for exactly `1` is wrong.

Each is a place where "it works" and "it is correct" differ — which is exactly why evaluators ask.

`ft_strncmp` `ft_memcmp` `ft_lstsize` `ft_lstmap` and more
defense: Why does `ft_strlcat` return `size + strlen(src)` in that branch?
return-contract.title: The return value is part of the specification, not an afterthought.

signed-char.body:
On x86 and ARM Linux, plain `char` is signed: −128 to 127. The byte `\200` reads as −128, so
`s1[i] - s2[i]` gives −128 where libc gives +128. Every comparison function in libc is specified
on `unsigned char`.

```
'\200' as   signed char  = -128    →  -128 - 0 < 0   ✗
'\200' as unsigned char  =  128    →   128 - 0 > 0   ✓
```
defense: Why did you cast to `unsigned char *` in `ft_memcmp`?
signed-char.title: A `char` may be signed. Memory functions compare bytes, not chars.

size-t-wrap.body:
```c
size_t n = 0;
n - 1;              /* 18446744073709551615, not -1 */
while (n--) { … }   /* runs once when n == 0 */
```

The common real instance is `ft_strlcat` computing `size - dstlen` without first checking
`size > dstlen`. When the destination is longer than the buffer, that subtraction wraps and the
copy loop writes until it hits an unmapped page.

`ft_strtrim` `ft_calloc` `ft_strncmp` `ft_memchr`

size-t-wrap.title: `size_t` is unsigned. Subtracting past zero gives a number near 18 quintillion.

string-literal-ro.body:
The literal lives in `.rodata`; writing through the pointer faults, with no warning at compile
time. `char s[] = "hello"` is a different thing entirely — an array, initialised from the
literal, writable.

It matters because `ft_striteri` takes `char *` and modifies in place: passing it a literal
crashes, and the crash is inside *your* function even though the bug is at the call site.
Pitfall **P2**.
defense: Why does `ft_striteri("hello", f)` crash when `ft_strmapi("hello", f)` does not?
string-literal-ro.title: `char *s = "hello"` points into read-only memory.

undefined-behavior.body:
Some inputs have no defined answer: `memcpy(NULL, NULL, 0)`, `strlcpy` with a `NULL` destination,
`atoi` past `INT_MAX`, signed overflow, writing to a literal. glibc survives several of them; the
42 Macs survive a different several. Neither is a specification.

These cases are run, displayed beside glibc's behaviour, labelled — and **never scored**.
Evaluators do poke them, and the right answer at defense is *"that is undefined behaviour; here
is what mine does and why I chose it"*, not silence.

`ft_putstr_fd`
about your code.
undefined-behavior.title: "It works on my machine" is not a defence, and neither is "libc does it".

defense.answer: `memcpy` is allowed to assume the source and destination do not overlap, and real implementations exploit that to copy in whatever order is fastest. If they do overlap the result is undefined. `memmove` guarantees a correct result either way: when `dst > src` it copies from the end backward, so it never overwrites a byte it still has to read.
defense.question: What is the difference between `memcpy` and `memmove`?

defense.answer: Subject IV.2 requires it to return a unique non-`NULL` pointer that can be passed to `free`. Returning `NULL` would make the caller unable to distinguish "you asked for nothing" from "allocation failed". `ft_calloc` also has to check `nmemb > SIZE_MAX / size` before multiplying — that overflow check is the reason `calloc` takes two arguments instead of one.
defense.question: Why does `ft_calloc` need to handle a zero argument?

defense.answer: Because `strlcat` reports the length it *tried* to build, so the caller can detect truncation. In that branch nothing can be appended, and `strlcat` cannot claim to know `strlen(dst)` — within the `size` it was given, `dst` was never `NUL`-terminated. So it reports the size it was allowed to consider plus the length it wanted to add.
defense.question: Why does `ft_strlcat` return `size + strlen(src)` when `size <= strlen(dst)`?

defense.answer: A 32-bit signed int holds −2147483648 to 2147483647, so +2147483648 does not exist. `n = -n` overflows, which is undefined behaviour, and in practice leaves the value negative. I handle it by <casting to long / using unsigned arithmetic / peeling the last digit before negating>.
defense.question: Why does `n = -2147483648` need special handling in `ft_putnbr_fd`?

defense.answer: `char` is signed on this architecture, so a byte above 127 reads as negative and the sign of a subtraction flips — `memcmp("\200", "\0", 1)` would return negative instead of positive. The standard defines these functions on `unsigned char`, so I cast once at the top and work in bytes.
defense.question: Why `unsigned char *` in `ft_memcmp` and `ft_memset`?

defense.answer: There are two levels. If the array of pointers fails, I return `NULL` immediately. If word *i* fails, words `0..i-1` are already allocated and nothing else in the program holds those pointers — so I free each of them, then the array, then return `NULL`. Every allocation index has to be handled, not just the first.
defense.question: Walk me through your malloc cleanup in `ft_split`.

defense.answer: Because the list does not own the contents in a way it understands. The caller allocated them and may have done so in a way plain `free` cannot undo — a nested structure, an array of allocations, a pool. `del` is the caller telling the list how to release one content. The nodes themselves are mine, so those I `free` directly.
defense.question: Why does `ft_lstclear` take `del`?

defense.answer: Because it has to change the caller's head pointer, and C passes arguments by value. With a `t_list *` I would only be reassigning my own local copy. The `**` gives me the address of the caller's variable so `*lst = new` writes through to it.

defense.answer: `strlen(s) - 1 + 1` bytes. `len` is a maximum, not a size — I cap it against the characters actually remaining after `start`. Trusting `len` would ask malloc for 18 exabytes and get `NULL`, which would look like an allocation failure rather than the arithmetic bug it is.

defense.answer: It is what `strchr` specifies — the return points into the original buffer, so the caller must not free or modify the string while holding it. That is also why the parameter is `const char *` and the return is `char *`: the standard's compromise so the function is usable from both `const` and non-`const` callers.
